name: Rafael Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Rafael, thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an orthopaedic trauma ward at the regional hospital, so mostly older people with broken hips, plus the odd motorbike crash. A day shift is six patients, lots of pain management, getting people up with the physios, watching for confusion after surgery and fighting with the bed manager. I'm also on the hospital's digital nursing group, so twice a month I test new software and tell the IT people what's useless.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love getting a ninety-year-old woman walking again three days after a new hip. What grinds me down is the duplication: I write the same thing in four places, and half of it nobody reads. I use AI tools every day at home, for studying and summarising research, and it drives me mad that the ward is ten years behind.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a rented flat ten minutes from the hospital. I've put money into index funds since I qualified, so I've got well over a year of cushion, and I pick up bank shifts on the high-pay weekends. I'm not in a hurry to buy anything or settle down yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Honestly that would disappoint me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because there were real gains on the table. At the digital group I'd still push for the small stuff, like auto-filled fluid charts. Online I'd probably admit I overhyped it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, nursing is nursing and my pay is good. But I'd be a bit bored. I was hoping the paperwork would finally shrink and I could spend more time on mobility and confused patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the ward, keep using AI for my own studying, and keep testing whatever the IT team sends. I'd probably start the part-time master's I've been eyeing anyway, maybe in advanced orthopaedic practice instead of informatics. Money stays in the index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat. Like a gadget you were excited about turning out to be a fancy timer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine task would you most want automated in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The falls-risk scoring we redo every shift. I fill in the same falls-risk form on the same patient three times a day, and nobody has ever read the third one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be bored. Would that push you to leave the ward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not leave nursing, no. Maybe towards advanced practice, so I can order X-rays and adjust pain plans myself. That's my backup plan if the tech stays dull.

say: I'd say real **gains** were on the table and it's a shame they didn't come.
I'd admit online that I had **overhyped** AI myself.
think: I'd be **fine**, since nursing pay is good and the work stays the same.
I'd be a bit **bored**, having hoped the **paperwork** would finally shrink.
do: Keep using **AI for studying** and testing the IT team's new software.
Start a **part-time master's** in advanced orthopaedic practice.
Leave savings in the **index funds** without changes.
feel: **Calm**, and a little flat, like an exciting gadget turned dull.
S0.quote: I fill in the same falls-risk form on the same patient three times a day, and nobody has ever read the third one.
fieldNote: He's the rare nurse who'd feel **disappointed** that AI stayed small.
His work and money are **secure**, so the plateau is about lost hope, not fear.
He names one exact **duplicated task**, the falls-risk form, as the thing worth fixing.

steps.text: Keep testing new ward software with the digital nursing group
Apply for the part-time master's in advanced orthopaedic practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's basically my dream version, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for nurses if the time saved goes back to patients. At the digital group I'd volunteer to lead the pilot on our ward. Online I'd post about what works and what doesn't, because I'd be one of the first using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it helps me. I'm the person on the ward who already understands the tools, so I'd become useful in a new way. My worry is for the healthcare assistants and the ward clerks, because the hospital will use the savings to cut them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up to be the ward's AI lead in the first month and run the charting pilot. I'd switch the master's to nursing informatics, which the hospital might part fund. I'd also bring it up at the union, because someone who likes the tech should be the one asking how the savings get shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. A little guilty about the people who'd lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our healthcare assistants, mostly. The tools I'm excited about could be the same tools the hospital uses to cut the healthcare assistants who do half the lifting on my ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You like the tech and you're in the union. Do those ever pull against each other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All the time. I want the tools, and I want the gains shared, and management only wants the first half. I'd push for a deal where time saved means more nurse hours with patients, not fewer staff.

say: I'd say AI is good for nurses if **saved time** goes back to **patients**.
I'd **post openly** about what works and what doesn't, as an early user.
think: I think it **helps me**, as the ward's person who already understands the tools.
I worry the hospital will cut **healthcare assistants** using the savings.
do: Volunteer as the ward's **AI lead** and run the **charting pilot** in month one.
Switch the master's to **nursing informatics**, ideally part funded by the hospital.
Raise **how savings are shared** at the union branch.
feel: **Calm and excited**, with some guilt about colleagues who'd lose out.
S1.quote: The tools I'm excited about could be the same tools the hospital uses to cut the healthcare assistants who do half the lifting on my ward.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as a **career opening**, not a threat.
He feels a real tension between **liking the tools** and protecting support staff.
He wants the union to have a **tech-friendly voice**, which he'd supply himself.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the AI charting pilot on the orthopaedic ward
Switch the master's to nursing informatics with hospital funding
Propose a union deal returning saved time to patient care

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking, then robots in 2031. That's a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public rules, fast, about who owns the gains, because private firms will grab it all. At work I'd tell people to learn the systems now, while humans still run them. Online I'd be arguing for some kind of shared dividend from AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's scarier than I'd admit. An informatics job is thinking work, so by 2028 the AI does that better than me too. My hands-on nursing keeps me until about 2031, and then I'm a guy with skills that a robot matches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still take the AI lead role, because being inside the change is better than outside it. But I'd drop the informatics master's, since it'd be outdated before I finished. I'd save harder, putting all bank shift money aside, and I'd get active in the union's national tech working group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Fascinated and scared at the same time, which is a weird mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean on your ward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2028 the AI does the falls scores, the pain plans, the discharge letters, and I'm basically hands for the system. For three years I'd be the hands for a computer that thinks better than me, and then the robots would make my hands optional too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a big cushion and you're young. Doesn't that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, and I'd say I'm luckier than most. But savings only matter if there's something to move to. If all thinking work goes in 2028, I don't know what I'd retrain into.

say: I'd call for **public rules** on who owns AI gains, before private firms take everything.
I'd tell colleagues to **learn the systems** while humans still run them.
think: I think **informatics** is thinking work, so AI beats me there by 2028 too.
My hands-on nursing keeps me until about **2031**, then robots match it.
do: Take the **AI lead** role anyway, to stay inside the change.
**Drop the informatics master's**, since it would be outdated before I finished.
Save **all bank shift money** and join the union's national tech working group.
feel: **Anxious**, with fascination and fear mixed together.
S2.quote: For three years I'd be the hands for a computer that thinks better than me, and then the robots would make my hands optional too.
fieldNote: Even the most **tech-keen** nurse here sees his backup career wiped out by fast AGI.
His savings help, but he can't name **anywhere to move** if thinking work goes.
He'd stay close to the **systems** rather than resist them, even when scared.

steps.text: Take the ward AI lead role and run the new system rollout
Put every bank shift payment into savings until 2031
Join the union's national working group on hospital technology

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to actually do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the window for governments to set up retraining and shared ownership properly. At work I'd run sessions showing colleagues how the tools work. Online I'd keep posting honest reviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd use the time to get into the jobs that last: the ones overseeing both the AI and the robots, and the very human bits of care. I think there'll be work for nurses who can run a ward full of machines safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the informatics master's fast, finishing by 2029, before AGI lands. I'd also take a course in robotics safety for clinical settings if one exists. I'd put more into the index funds, since if the economy grows from all this I want a slice of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. It's a race I think I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the years before 2031, while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who knows how to keep patients safe around robots. If robots are coming to my ward by 2034, I want to be the nurse who wrote the rulebook for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about shared ownership but also putting money in index funds. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I want public ownership of the gains, but until that happens I'm not going to sit on cash while shareholders get rich. I'd vote one way and invest the other, and I'm fine admitting that.

say: I'd say **five years** is the window for proper retraining and **shared ownership**.
I'd run **sessions** showing colleagues how the new tools work.
think: I'd aim for jobs that **oversee** both the AI and the **robots**.
I think nurses who can run a **ward full of machines** safely will still have work.
do: Finish the **informatics master's** by 2029, before AGI lands.
Take a **clinical robotics safety** course if one exists.
Put **more into index funds** to get a slice of any growth.
S3.quote: If robots are coming to my ward by 2034, I want to be the nurse who wrote the rulebook for them.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **race** he believes he can win.
He openly owns the tension between **public ownership** views and private investing.
His plan is unusually specific: **robot safety** rules for wards.

steps.text: Finish the nursing informatics master's before 2029
Enrol in a clinical robotics safety course
Raise monthly index fund payments with bank shift earnings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind with a decade's notice. I'd push the hospital to start training everyone now, not in 2035. Online I'd keep being the annoying optimist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I'm twenty-seven, I'd have time to do a master's, maybe a second one, and land somewhere senior by the time robots arrive. My worry is more about older colleagues who'd retire just as their pensions wobble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the informatics master's at a normal pace and aim for a clinical lead job by about 2032. I might try a year working abroad, maybe in a hospital that's ahead on robotics. I'd keep investing steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious about what it'll look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why work abroad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To see it before it hits here. I'd rather spend a year on a ward that already has robots than read about them in a staff newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned older colleagues. Anyone in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our ward sister, Margaret, is fifty-six and brilliant at the bedside. She'd be fine with ten years, mostly, but she's terrified of computers. I'd want to help her through it.

say: I'd say a **decade's notice** means nobody should be **left behind**.
I'd push the hospital to **train everyone now**, not in 2035.
think: I think I'd **do well**, reaching a senior role before robots arrive.
I worry more about **older colleagues** whose pensions might wobble near retirement.
do: Do the informatics master's at a normal pace, aiming for **clinical lead** by 2032.
Spend a year **working abroad** on a ward already using robots.
feel: **Calm** and curious about what the change will look like.
S4.quote: I'd rather spend a year on a ward that already has robots than read about them in a staff newsletter.
fieldNote: With ten years his worry shifts entirely to **other people**, like his ward sister.
He'd go **abroad** to see robots first, a classic early-adopter move.
His plan is a **career ladder**, not a defence.

steps.text: Complete the nursing informatics master's part time by 2030
Apply for a one-year post on a robot-equipped ward abroad
Keep monthly index fund contributions steady

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my backup plan, informatics, disappears along with the nursing. Fast AGI would make my backup plan useless before I'd finished training for it. What would help is public ownership of some of the gains, a real dividend, and paid time to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether nurses get a say in what the robots do. The people designing these things have never done a night on an ortho ward with three confused patients trying to climb out of bed.

headlineQuote: Fast AGI would make my backup plan useless before I'd finished training for it.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old** orthopaedic trauma nurse who uses **AI tools daily** and tests ward software.
He lives alone in a rented flat with **over a year** of savings in index funds.
He's **calm** in AI Plateau, Steady Disruption and AGI by 2036, seeing them as career openings.
AGI by 2028 makes him **anxious**, because his backup plan in informatics is thinking work too.
He wants AI gains **publicly shared** while openly investing privately in the meantime.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, which wipes out his **informatics** backup plan along with nursing.
whatWouldHelp: **Public ownership** of some AI gains, paid as a dividend.
**Paid time** to retrain while still working.
